questions.passage: Some critics allege that current agricultural certification requirements and procedures, while uniform in application, are _____ in effect. The extensive paperwork requirements and high costs associated with certification can easily be absorbed by global agriculture companies with vast resources, whereas they can represent a significant burden for small farms.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: salutary
inequitable
negligible
indeterminate
questions.why: The same rules weigh lightly on large companies and heavily on small farms: unequal in effect.

questions.passage: Studying sales and price data for 325 brands of cooking sauces, cat food, bath additives, and other consumer packaged goods, Koushyar Rajavi and colleagues found that pricing, though hardly _____ brand success, made a much less pronounced contribution to brand success than retail distribution breadth did.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: determinative of
contingent on
uncharacteristic of
immaterial to
questions.why: Pricing still contributed, just less: "hardly irrelevant to" success.

questions.passage: Difficulties of documenting nocturnal pollinator visits and a general focus on diurnal invertebrate pollinators, such as Andrena dorsata, have resulted in _____ of information on nocturnal moth pollination of plants such as Rubus fruticosus L. aggregate, but Max Anderson et al. have addressed this by utilizing infrared technology.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: an aggregation
a dearth
a dissonance
an abatement
questions.why: Difficulty and neglect leave a shortage of information, which Anderson et al. then addressed.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from the 1895 poem “The Song My Paddle Sings” by Emily Pauline Johnson (Tekahionwake).

West wind blow from your prairie nest,
Blow from the mountains, blow from the west.
The sail is idle, the sailor too;
O! wind of the west, we wait for you.
questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “idle” most nearly mean?
choices: Frivolous
Untrustworthy
Unsupported
Inactive
questions.why: Without wind the sail does nothing; the speaker waits.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Virginia Woolf’s 1919 novel Night and Day. Katharine is the granddaughter of a celebrated poet.

[Katharine’s] descent from [a celebrated poet] was no surprise to her, but matter for satisfaction, until, as the years wore on, certain drawbacks made themselves very manifest. Perhaps it is a little depressing to inherit not lands but an example of intellectual virtue; perhaps the conclusiveness of a great ancestor is a little discouraging to those who run the risk of comparison with him.
questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “manifest” most nearly mean?
choices: Complex
Evident
Anticipated
Particular
questions.why: The drawbacks became very apparent, as the next sentence goes on to name them.
flags: Watermark covered 'satisfaction, ___, as the years'; restored as 'until' (Woolf's original wording).

questions.passage: According to a study led by Claire Heeryung Kim, artifact emojis—pictorial symbols representing objects, such as a flower—generally elicit consumer skepticism when used in digital marketing messages. However, the effect was found to be moderated by the emojis’ relevance to the message content: for instance, a pizza company’s email about football and pizza prompted less skepticism when it included football and pizza symbols than when it included gift-box and speaker symbols. This suggests that, barring avoidance of artifact emojis altogether, marketers would benefit from selecting symbols based on their pertinence.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain that inconsistent use of artifact emojis across digital marketing communications undermines consumers’ trust in and willingness to engage with a company
To illustrate why artifact emojis typically prompt consumer skepticism when they are incorporated into digital marketing communications
To present research findings about consumer responses to artifact emojis that point to a recommendation for more effective implementation in marketing messages
To contrast two methodological approaches researchers used in a study to measure consumer responses to the inclusion of artifact emojis in different forms of marketing messages
questions.why: Findings (skepticism, moderated by relevance) lead to a recommendation (pick pertinent symbols).

questions.passage:
Text 1

The island of Grande Terre split from the former supercontinent Gondwana around 80 million years ago, carrying Gondwanan species from a variety of clades with it. The island was periodically submerged until 37 million years ago, but some researchers suggest that its current biota includes species from clades predating the split that took refuge on islands near Grande Terre during submergence events and then returned.

Text 2

Prashant Sharma and Gonzalo Giribet found that the crown age—the age of the most recent common ancestor of all species in the clade (i.e., the clade’s founder)—of Grande Terre’s clade of harvest spiders is 48.9 million years, which is among the oldest clade crown ages of species inhabiting the island today. Nearly all of Grande Terre’s living species belong to clades that originated much more recently: for example, the crown age of the island’s clade of winter’s bark plants is 15.0 million years.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement about the “Gondwanan species” discussed in Text 1?
choices: Few if any of them were members of a clade that includes species currently inhabiting Grande Terre.
Although most of them have living descendants on Grande Terre, the harvest spiders and winter’s bark plants do not.
Most of them began recolonizing Grande Terre from nearby islands around 15.0 million years ago.
Clades to which they belong originated no earlier than 48.9 million years ago.
questions.why: The split was 80 million years ago, yet even the oldest living clades founded 48.9 million years ago; so the clades on the island today postdate the Gondwanan species.
flags: Stem cut off in the screenshot; taken from the user's message.
Watermark covered '80 ___ years' (million) and 'the ___ recent common ancestor' (most); restored.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Brown University and the investment bank Barclays are two of the many institutions offering training programs in entrepreneurship. But what results do such programs produce? In a study of business school graduates in Norway, researchers Lars Kolvereid and Øystein Moen addressed this question and convincingly demonstrated that participants showed strong intentions to become entrepreneurs as a result of receiving entrepreneurial training.

Text 2

While studies of entrepreneurial training typically report positive results, a close look at these studies reveals widespread methodological shortcomings. For instance, a 1997 study by Lars Kolvereid and Øystein Moen found benefits of entrepreneurial education for graduates of Norwegian business schools, but the study only collected data on subjects after the training, not before, making it unclear whether the training actually had an effect.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, the author of Text 1 and the author of Text 2 would most likely disagree about the answer to which question?
choices: Is the cost of conducting entrepreneurial training programs typically offset by the programs’ benefits?
Did Kolvereid and Moen’s study provide persuasive evidence that its results are attributable to the entrepreneurial training participants received?
Did Kolvereid and Moen report that participants who received the entrepreneurial training showed strong intentions to become entrepreneurs?
Are there convincing experimental results showing that different types of entrepreneurial training programs are associated with different outcomes?
questions.why: Text 1 says the study convincingly showed the training caused the intentions; Text 2 says data only after training leaves the effect unclear. Both agree on what was reported (C).

questions.passage: “Coyote” is one example of an English word that has an indigenous origin. The word came to English indirectly from coyote, the Spanish word for the wild canine species. Spanish had borrowed it from Nahuatl, an Indigenous language of Central Mexico, in which the word’s original form is coyotl. “Iguana” also has an indigenous origin and entered English through Spanish. But in this case, the original source was Taino, a language of the Caribbean islands, in which the word for the group of related lizard species is iwana.
questions.stem: According to the text, what is one difference between the English words “coyote” and “iguana”?
choices: “Coyote” is known for being indigenous in origin, while “iguana” is mistakenly regarded as Spanish in origin.
“Coyote” changed in meaning significantly when English borrowed the word from Spanish, whereas “iguana” retained its original meaning.
“Coyote” can be traced to the Nahuatl language, while “iguana” can be traced to the Taino language.
“Coyote” entered English recently, but “iguana” entered English many centuries ago.
questions.why: Both came through Spanish from indigenous languages; the stated difference is the source language: Nahuatl vs Taino.

questions.passage: Models indicate that when Neptune captured its moon Triton, the moon first entered a stretched, elongated orbit and could have stayed bound to Neptune only by quickly shedding orbital energy. Researchers long assumed that tidal interactions between Triton and Neptune enabled that shedding, gradually reshaping Triton’s orbit to its current path. Newer work suggests that as Triton passed through a crowd of moons circling Neptune, tides would have acted too slowly to keep it bound. Collisions with those moons, however, could have dissipated orbital energy roughly ten times faster than tides could have.
questions.stem: Based on the text, how might collisions with Neptune’s existing moons have affected Triton?
choices: By allowing Triton to shed orbital energy fast enough to keep the moon bound to Neptune
By enabling a sufficiently rapid reduction in Triton’s orbital energy to preserve the moon’s initial orbit
By enabling Triton to remain bound to Neptune despite a rapid loss in orbital energy
By slowing the stretching and elongation of Triton’s orbit so the moon would not drift toward Neptune
questions.why: Collisions shed energy ten times faster than tides, fast enough to keep Triton bound. B says the orbit was preserved (it was reshaped); C reverses cause and effect.
flags: Watermark covered 'assumed that ___ interactions between ___ and Neptune'; restored as 'tidal' and 'Triton'.

questions.passage: Orbicella faveolata, a Caribbean coral with a boulder-like shape, and Pocillopora eydouxi, a coral from the Indian Ocean with branching clusters, are both stony corals—the type that builds reefs. Increasing stony coral colonies worldwide is a key objective for ecologists, since land-based runoff and other pressures are causing growing harm to reefs. In the wild, crustose coralline algae (CCA) promote growth in the healthy reefs they inhabit by releasing lipids and other metabolites—chemical cues that trigger coral larvae settlement. Biotechnology researcher Lina Haddad and team have developed a tool to restore those cues in damaged reefs: a gel coating infused with metabolites derived from Indian Ocean CCA. In tests with Porites lutea, an Indian Ocean stony coral, settlement rates rose substantially.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would best support a claim that the new tool already has the capacity to support the scope of the ecologists’ objective?
choices: The lipids and other metabolites derived from Indian Ocean CCA seem to remain stable for long periods under a variety of water temperatures and environmental conditions.

Exposure to lipids and other metabolites released by CCA from Indian Ocean reefs improves settlement rates for larvae of Orbicella faveolata and a variety of other coral species in regions outside the Indian Ocean.
In Indian Ocean reefs, higher concentrations of lipids and other metabolites released by local CCA are linked to larger colonies of Pocillopora eydouxi and greater overall diversity of coral species.
When CCA are present and releasing lipids and other metabolites, larvae settlement rates improve nearly as much in damaged reefs with Porites lutea as they do in healthy reefs containing that coral.
questions.why: The objective is worldwide, but the gel was tested only on an Indian Ocean coral; B shows the same Indian Ocean metabolites working for corals elsewhere.

questions.passage: In countries with right-hand traffic, drivers who want to make a left turn at a traffic intersection with stoplights have to wait for either a gap in oncoming traffic or a designated left-turn signal to turn green. At busy intersections, this often causes a backup of vehicles waiting to turn left or being prevented from proceeding by left-turning vehicles in front of them. Transportation researcher Vikash V. Gayah claims that in urban areas eliminating the option to turn left at busy intersections—both with and without dedicated left-turn signals—would improve traffic flow and, as a result, reduce overall travel times even if such a restriction would require drivers to sometimes travel a slightly longer distance.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher’s claim?
choices: In a town that installed left-turn signals at all busy intersections, seven out of ten survey respondents agreed with the statement “the streets in my community are easier to navigate by motor vehicle than before.”

After a city eliminated left turns at busy intersections, a package-delivery company reports that its drivers have been able to reach more addresses in the city daily, on average, and therefore deliver more packages there annually.

Statistics reveal that school buses in a city that eliminated left turns at most intersections took on average two minutes longer to complete their routes after the restriction took effect than they did before.
A traffic study of intersections in a large city shows that on average drivers wait longer to make a left turn at intersections without left-turn signals than at intersections with such signals.
questions.why: More stops per day after left turns were banned means shorter overall travel time despite longer routes. C would weaken; A and D are not about eliminating left turns.

questions.passage: “Golden Hours” by Clara J. Whitmore, published in the Chicago Evening Post in 1878, exemplifies the phenomenon of “fugitive verse,” poems reprinted in newspapers and other nineteenth-century US periodicals without authorial oversight or even, in many cases, knowledge. Though poems that became fugitive verse were typical of newspaper poetry of their era in their reliance on such elements as simple rhyme schemes and everyday settings, the phenomenon of fugitive verse represents a significant departure from the dominant model of literary authorship in which a work is controlled by a single and publicly identified author. This practice, however, was accepted as routine, even by the poets affected; that it has come to seem anomalous is indicative of the fact that _____
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the authors of nineteenth-century newspaper poetry placed less value on artistic control than did their contemporaries who wrote other types of literature.
the concept of authorship and the privileges associated with the author’s role are mediated by the contexts within which works are written and published.
the notion that authors should have control over the reprinting of their works was a contested issue in nineteenth-century literary culture.
the literary characteristics of works disseminated through commercial venues are influenced by the circumstances of publication as well as by authorial choices.
questions.why: Routine then, anomalous now: what counts as an author's control depends on the setting of writing and publication. C contradicts "accepted as routine"; D is about literary features, not authorship.

questions.passage: Indigenous songs can be repositories of ecological information, from Yi songs about the natural environment to Tlingit songs about wildlife encounters. Kwakwaka’wakw song keeper Kwaxsistalla Wathl’thla aided research by ethnobiologist Dana Lepofsky et al. by contributing songs that reference creating terraced intertidal gardens to foster the healthy development of clams, a staple in the Kwakwaka’wakw people’s diet. Such structures date as far back as 3,500 years ago. Intriguingly, analysis of local paleoecological marine bivalve records has revealed significant increases in clam size and productivity as clam garden practices became more prevalent and harvesting pressure increased—a finding that bolsters the notion that _____
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the Kwakwaka’wakw people encouraged the health of clam gardens and reduced pressure on them by periodically increasing their reliance on other sources of sustenance.
the practical approach described in the Kwakwaka’wakw songs effectively maintained clams as a sustainable food source.
the Kwakwaka’wakw people initially adapted their clam garden practices from similar methods observed among other Indigenous peoples in neighboring areas.
contemporary Kwakwaka’wakw people have only minimally deviated from the clam-gardening practices described in the people’s songs.
questions.why: Clams got bigger and more productive even as harvesting rose, so the gardening the songs describe kept the food source sustainable. A contradicts "harvesting pressure increased".

record—evidence of cloning in
record, evidence of cloning, in
